name: Germany
score_rationale: LAND stays 1: ownership is nationality-neutral but farmland averages USD 40,000/ha (USD 17,000 in the cheapest eastern states) and GrdstVG approval plus Landgesellschaft pre-emption can block non-farmer buyers. VISA stays 1: no passive-income, golden or nomad visa; retirees depend on discretionary section 7 permits and private insurance; the only group-friendly route is forming a farm business under section 21 or sponsoring skilled workers; citizenship 5 years with dual nationality allowed, but the 3-year fast track died in Oct 2025. TAX stays 1: worldwide taxation at 45 percent plus soli, no wealth tax, crypto 1-year exemption still live but slated for a 25 percent flat tax from 2027. LAW stays 2: the eG, Stiftung/Erbbaurecht and Mietshaeuser Syndikat models are the best communal vehicles in the atlas, but section 35 BauGB zoning denies new housing on open farmland, which caps the score. LIFE stays 3 (HDI 0.959, WJP 0.83, Numbeo QoL 200.85, universal healthcare). STAB stays 3 (FSI 24.0, CPI 77, ND-GAIN 3rd) despite the GPI slide from 20th to 28th in 2026.
verdict: Gold-standard co-op law and stability, but land is expensive, building is strict, and there's no easy passive-income visa.
summary: Germany has the world's most mature legal toolkit for communal land (the eingetragene Genossenschaft, Stiftung-plus-Erbbaurecht models like Stiftung trias, the Mietshaeuser Syndikat) and top-tier stability, but farmland averages EUR 35,300/ha (about USD 40,000; eastern states about EUR 15,000/ha), sales of farmland are subject to Grundstueckverkehrsgesetz approval that can favour local farmers, and you cannot build new housing on open farmland (section 35 BauGB) unless you are a bona fide farm business, so plan on buying an existing farmstead or village site. Non-EU members have no passive-income or golden visa: each person needs an individual basis (section 21 self-employment, Blue Card or skilled-worker permit, or a discretionary section 7 retiree permit) plus full health insurance; permanent residence takes 3 to 5 years and citizenship 5 years (the 3-year fast track was repealed on 30 Oct 2025). Taxation is worldwide at up to 45 percent plus 5.5 percent solidarity surcharge, with no wealth tax and crypto still tax-free after a one-year hold, though the government is drafting a 25 percent flat crypto tax for 2027.

land.text: East-German depopulation, but farmland pricey (~€26k/ha) & strict
land.house: Rare cheap-village stock in the east; no formal program
land.ownership_note: Nationality is irrelevant: EU and non-EU persons and foreign-owned companies can hold German farmland freehold on the same terms as Germans. The real constraint is structural, not national. Under the Grundstueckverkehrsgesetz (GrdstVG) every sale of agricultural or forestry land above a state-set threshold (0.15 ha in Saarland up to 2 ha in Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt and Schleswig-Holstein; Baden-Wuerttemberg has its own ASVG) needs approval from the agricultural authority, which can be refused under section 9 GrdstVG for an 'ungesunde Verteilung des Grund und Bodens' (typically a sale to a non-farmer when a local full-time farmer needs the land), an uneconomic split (agricultural parcels below 1 ha, forest below 3.5 ha) or a price grossly above market value. For parcels of 2 ha or more the non-profit Landgesellschaft holds a statutory pre-emption right under section 4 Reichssiedlungsgesetz when approval would otherwise be refused. A group that registers as a farm business (eG or GmbH actually farming the land) is treated as a farmer for these purposes; buying an existing farmstead with buildings (Hofstelle) or leasing (Pacht; arable rents average roughly EUR 400/ha/yr) are the common workarounds. Prices (Destatis 2024): national average EUR 35,300/ha for all agricultural land, arable EUR 42,800, grassland EUR 24,800; West EUR 53,500 vs East EUR 16,800; cheapest states Brandenburg EUR 14,915, Thuringia EUR 14,926, Saarland EUR 15,042, Saxony EUR 17,789; dearest North Rhine-Westphalia EUR 97,727 and Bavaria EUR 94,415.
land.build_rules: GrdstVG section 9 presumes an uneconomic split if an agricultural parcel would fall below 1 ha or forest below 3.5 ha, so micro-parcelling land among members can be refused. New dwellings in the Aussenbereich (outside the built-up area or a Bebauungsplan) are only permitted under section 35(1) BauGB if they 'serve' an agricultural or forestry business and occupy a subordinate part of its land; section 35(4) allows conversion of preserved farm buildings into at most 5 additional dwellings per farmstead if the exterior is kept and the building was not abandoned more than 7 years.
land.cheap_house_program: None. There is no national or state 'one-euro house' scheme. Cheap village stock exists in depopulating eastern districts (Brandenburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) where whole farmsteads and manor complexes (e.g. Schloss Tonndorf 2005, Hof Praedikow 2016) were bought by groups, but each is an ordinary private purchase subject to GrdstVG approval and real-estate transfer tax of 3.5 to 6.5 percent.
land.note: Land is expensive by global standards but the East-West gap is huge: USD 17,000/ha in Brandenburg or Thuringia vs USD 110,000/ha in NRW. Rents are a cheaper entry (arable rents about EUR 400/ha/yr) and long-term Pacht contracts are standard. Property purchase also triggers Grunderwerbsteuer (3.5 to 6.5 percent) and notary/registry fees; Grundsteuer (annual property tax) was re-based from 1 Jan 2025.

visas.name: Residence permit for self-employment / entrepreneur (section 21(1) AufenthG)
visas.requirement: A business plan showing (1) an economic interest or regional need, (2) expected positive effects on the economy, and (3) secured financing via own capital or a loan commitment; no statutory minimum capital or job count since the 2012 reform of section 21. Applicants over 45 must show adequate old-age provision (section 21(3)). A registered farm business or eco-village enterprise (eG/GmbH) can be the vehicle for several founding members. Practical livelihood proof of roughly EUR 2,000 to 2,500 net per month per adult is expected by most missions.
visas.initial_term: Up to 3 years (section 21(4)), renewable while the business is viable
visas.processing_time: Typically 6 to 12 weeks at the embassy, up to 3 to 6 months in slow missions; the embassy must decide within 3 months (section 75 VwGO)

visas.name: Freelancer residence permit (section 21(5) AufenthG, Freiberufler)
visas.requirement: Liberal profession (artists, writers, IT consultants, teachers, architects, physicians etc.) with any licence required; proof of clients/contracts and income sufficient to live without public funds, in practice about EUR 2,000 to 2,500 net per month in cities, less in rural areas; proof of health insurance; over-45s show pension provision. Note: the 3-year settlement path of section 21(4) does NOT apply to freelancers; they go through the general 5-year rule of section 9.
visas.processing_time: 6 to 12 weeks typical; 60 to 180 days depending on consulate

visas.name: EU Blue Card (section 18g AufenthG)
visas.requirement: Recognised university degree plus a job offer of at least 6 months paying at least EUR 50,700 gross per year in 2026 (EUR 45,934.20 for shortage occupations such as IT, engineering, medicine, and for graduates within 3 years of their degree). Thresholds are 50 percent / 45.3 percent of the pension contribution ceiling (EUR 101,400 in 2026) and reset every January.
visas.initial_term: Up to 4 years (or contract length plus 3 months)
visas.processing_time: 4 to 12 weeks; accelerated procedure available via employer

visas.name: Skilled worker residence permit (sections 18a/18b AufenthG) with settlement under section 18c
visas.requirement: Recognised vocational or academic qualification plus a concrete job offer in Germany (agricultural employers can sponsor, e.g. an organic farm or eco-village enterprise); Federal Employment Agency consent; secured livelihood. Settlement permit after 36 months of residence permit and pension contributions (24 months if trained in Germany) with sufficient German; Blue Card holders after 27 months or 21 months with B1 German.

visas.name: Opportunity Card / Chancenkarte (section 20a AufenthG, job-search permit, since June 2024)
visas.requirement: Either a fully recognised foreign qualification, or at least 6 points under the points system plus a state-recognised vocational qualification of at least 2 years or a degree and at least A1 German or B2 English; livelihood must be secured (blocked account at the standard rate set by the authorities; verify the current monthly figure with the embassy). Allows part-time work of at most 20 hours per week on average and 2-week trial jobs; converts to a skilled-worker or Blue Card permit once a qualified job is found; extendable by up to 2 years only if a qualified job contract is obtained.

visas.name: Retiree / person of independent means residence permit (section 7(1) sentence 3 AufenthG, discretionary)
visas.requirement: No dedicated retirement visa exists; section 7(1) s.3 lets the Auslaenderbehoerde grant a permit 'in begruendeten Faellen' for a purpose not listed in the Act. No statutory income floor: authorities expect passive income or assets clearly above the subsistence level, in practice at least about EUR 1,200 to 1,500 per month plus rent, full German-standard health insurance (third-country retirees usually cannot join statutory GKV and must buy private cover; applicants over roughly 75 may be refused by insurers), adequate housing and ties to Germany. Grant is discretionary and varies by district; retirees in rural depopulating districts often get a friendlier hearing. Permanent settlement after 5 years under section 9 requires 60 months of statutory pension contributions or comparable private provision, B1 German and civic knowledge.
visas.initial_term: 1 year, renewable (typically 1 to 2 years per renewal)
visas.processing_time: 2 to 4 months at the embassy; several months at local offices

visas.name: Digital nomad visa
visas.requirement: Germany has no digital-nomad visa. Remote workers must use the freelancer permit (section 21(5)) with German clients or a German business footprint, the Chancenkarte, or a skilled-worker route; remote employment for a foreign employer alone is not a recognised purpose of residence. EU/EEA/Swiss citizens need no permit at all.

visas.name: Restoration of citizenship for descendants of Nazi-era persecution (Art. 116(2) Basic Law and section 15 StAG) and declaration route (section 5 StAG)
visas.requirement: Descendants of persons deprived of German citizenship on political, racial or religious grounds between 30 Jan 1933 and 8 May 1945 (and, under section 15 StAG, of those who were excluded from acquiring it) can claim German citizenship by declaration with no residence, language or renunciation requirement. Section 5 StAG also lets children born before 1 Jan 2000 to a German parent who could not pass on citizenship under old gender-discriminatory rules (and their descendants) acquire citizenship by declaration until 19 Aug 2031. German citizens are EU citizens with full settlement and work rights.
visas.processing_time: Typically 1 to 3 years at the Bundesverwaltungsamt

visa_text: Freelancer/self-employ, skilled-worker; citizenship now 5y
visa_detail: Freelancer/self-employed or skilled-worker visa; income-proof. ~1–3 mo. Settlement ~5 yr (fast-track 3) · citizenship now 5 yr.
visa_note: EU/EEA/Swiss citizens simply register (Anmeldung) and can buy land and farm immediately. For third-country members there is no passive-income, rentista, golden or digital-nomad visa and no investor minimum; the realistic group strategy is to form the farm/eco-village enterprise first (eG or GmbH) and bring founders in under section 21(1) (settlement after 3 years) and employees under skilled-worker/Blue Card permits (settlement after 21 to 36 months), with retirees on discretionary section 7 permits. Since the Staatsangehoerigkeitsmodernisierungsgesetz of 27 June 2024, naturalisation needs 5 years of lawful residence, B1 German, secured livelihood and a civics test, and dual citizenship is allowed; the 3-year fast track for 'special integration' was repealed with effect from 30 Oct 2025 (Bundestag vote 8 Oct 2025, 450 to 134). Spouses of Germans still qualify after 3 years. Processing is slow at many Auslaenderbehoerden (months) even when embassy decisions are fast.

tax.text: Income to 45%; no wealth tax; crypto 0% after 1yr hold
tax.capital_gains: Investment income (interest, dividends, gains on securities) is taxed at a flat 25 percent plus 5.5 percent solidarity surcharge = 26.375 percent (plus church tax if a member), withheld at source, with a EUR 1,000 saver's allowance per person (EUR 2,000 for couples). Private sale transactions: movable assets including crypto are tax-free if held more than 1 year, otherwise taxed at the progressive rate; gains are exempt if total private-sale gains in the year are under EUR 1,000. Real estate is tax-free after a 10-year holding period (or if owner-occupied in the year of sale and the two prior years).
tax.wealth_tax: None (suspended since 1997). Inheritance and gift tax is progressive at 7 to 50 percent with allowances of EUR 20,000 to 500,000 depending on relationship; transfers of business and agricultural assets enjoy substantial relief.
tax.property_tax: Grundsteuer (annual, municipal) was re-based from 1 Jan 2025 under the new valuation law (federal model or state variants); amounts are modest for rural land and houses but depend on the municipal Hebesatz. Grundsteuer A applies to agricultural land. Real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) of 3.5 to 6.5 percent of the price is due on every purchase, varying by state.
tax.foreign_pension: German tax residents are taxed on worldwide pension income. Under the US-Germany treaty US Social Security paid to a German resident is taxable only in Germany (Art. 18(5)); private pensions, IRAs and 401(k) distributions are taxable in the residence state (Art. 18/18A); government-service pensions stay taxable in the paying state (Art. 19). From the 2025 assessment period, foreign pensions whose contributions were tax-privileged abroad are fully taxable in Germany (confirmed by the Federal Fiscal Court for US plans). UK state and public-service pensions follow the UK-Germany treaty. No special low-tax regime for inbound retirees exists.
tax.special_regime: No inbound flat-tax, non-dom or lump-sum regime. Solidarity surcharge of 5.5 percent on income tax applies only above an income-tax burden of about EUR 19,950 (single) / 39,900 (joint); church tax 8 to 9 percent of income tax if registered as a member. Married couples can split income (Ehegattensplitting). Top rate 45 percent applies above EUR 277,826 taxable income (2025); the 42 percent band starts at EUR 68,430.
tax.crypto: Private crypto gains are tax-free after a holding period of more than 12 months (section 23 EStG one-year rule), otherwise taxed at progressive rates up to 45 percent with a EUR 1,000 annual exemption. Flag for 2027: a federal cabinet position adopted in July 2026 points to moving crypto gains into the 25 percent flat investment-income regime from 2027 (effective 26.375 percent with soli); as of 10 Sep 2026 no statutory text had been published and the one-year exemption remains in force.
tax.coop_treatment: An eingetragene Genossenschaft is a corporation taxed at 15 percent corporate tax plus 5.5 percent soli and municipal trade tax, but section 5(1) no. 14 KStG fully exempts agricultural and forestry cooperatives and associations whose activities are confined to shared use of farm equipment, services, processing or marketing of members' own agricultural products (non-member/other revenue must stay at or below 10 percent of total). Bodies recognised as gemeinnuetzig (charitable, e.g. an e.V., gGmbH or Stiftung for education/ecology) are exempt under section 5(1) no. 9 KStG and can issue donation receipts.

cost.note: About EUR 1,300 to 1,700 per adult per month in a small town or village (2026 prices): rent EUR 400 to 800 for a one-bedroom outside city centres (far less, or zero, when living on a bought farmstead), groceries EUR 200 to 300, utilities EUR 150 to 200, health insurance from about EUR 270 per month for a self-employed person on the minimum assessment base (private cover averages about EUR 520), transport EUR 60 to 100 for a pass or EUR 170 to 350 with a car. National single-person averages are EUR 1,800 to 2,500 including big-city rents; Saarbruecken-type small cities run roughly 40 percent below Munich.

health.system: Bismarck-model dual system: statutory health insurance (GKV, about 90 percent of residents, income-based premiums, family members co-insured free) alongside substitutive private insurance (PKV, risk-rated premiums). Insurance is compulsory for every resident from day one, and proof of cover is a condition of every residence permit.
health.cost_for_residents: GKV 2026: 14.6 percent (14.0 percent without sick-pay entitlement) plus an insurer-specific supplementary contribution averaging 2.9 percent plus 3.6 percent long-term care (4.2 percent if childless over 23), i.e. about 21 percent of income; employees split this with the employer, the self-employed pay all of it on a minimum assessment base of EUR 1,316.67/month (minimum premium about EUR 270/month) up to the ceiling of EUR 5,812.50/month (maximum about EUR 1,200/month). Private cover averages about EUR 520/month and rises with age. Out-of-pocket co-pays are small (EUR 10 per prescription, capped at 2 percent of income).
health.immigrant_access: Employees are enrolled in GKV automatically. Self-employed arrivals can join GKV voluntarily only if they move their permanent residence to Germany, register the activity, and apply within 3 months of leaving a prior (EU/EEA/treaty-state or German) insurance; otherwise they must take PKV or an expat policy. Third-country retirees and passive-income holders usually cannot enter GKV and must buy private cover that meets section 193 VVG standards; insurers may refuse applicants over about 75 or with pre-existing conditions, which can block the section 7 retiree permit. Once in, access to care is identical to citizens.
health.quality_note: Dense rural GP and hospital network, though rural GP shortages are growing in the east; HDI life expectancy 81.4 years; Numbeo healthcare index 71.25 (Oct 2026).

pension.foreign_pension_tax: Taxed as ordinary income at progressive rates up to 45 percent plus soli once resident; US Social Security and private pensions are taxable only in Germany under the US-Germany treaty (Art. 18(5), 18/18A), government-service pensions only in the paying state (Art. 19); since the 2025 assessment period foreign pensions built from tax-privileged contributions are 100 percent taxable (BFH ruling on US plans). No remittance or flat-rate concession for foreign retirees; the basic allowance is EUR 12,096 (2025).
pension.retiree_visa: None dedicated. Retirees apply under the discretionary section 7(1) sentence 3 AufenthG 'other purpose' permit: show passive income/assets comfortably above subsistence (in practice about EUR 1,200 to 1,500/month plus rent), private health insurance meeting German standards, and housing; 1-year renewable permits, no work; permanent residence after 5 years under section 9 requires 60 months of statutory pension contributions or comparable private provision plus B1 German, which many retirees never satisfy. Processing 2 to 4 months at the embassy.

ag.subsidies: EU CAP 2023-2027 direct payments (GAP-Direktzahlungen) are open to any active farmer with eligible land, regardless of nationality or legal form. 2025 unit rates: basic income support (Einkommensgrundstuetzung) EUR 152.44/ha; redistributive top-up EUR 68.05/ha for the first 40 ha and EUR 40.83/ha for ha 41-60 (favours small farms); young-farmer top-up EUR 120.64/ha for up to 120 ha for a maximum of 5 years (farmer under 41); voluntary eco-schemes (Oeko-Regelungen) EUR 40 to 1,300/ha depending on measure (e.g. non-productive arable set-aside, flower strips, agroforestry, organic). 2026 planned rates: EUR 147.38 basic, EUR 65.31/39.19 redistributive, EUR 134.04 young farmer. Second-pillar organic conversion and maintenance premiums and agri-environment payments are run by each Land. Applications go through the annual Gemeinsamer Antrag (deadline 15 May).
ag.coop_law: Genossenschaftsgesetz (GenG) of 1889, in force in its current version: section 1 defines the eingetragene Genossenschaft (eG) as a society of unlimited membership whose purpose is to promote members' economic interests or, since the 2006 amendment, their social or cultural concerns through a joint business; section 4 requires at least 3 members; the eG must belong to a cooperative auditing federation (Pruefungsverband). Agricultural eGs are corporate-tax exempt under section 5(1) no. 14 KStG if non-member business stays within 10 percent. Germany's Raiffeisen cooperative tradition dates to the 1860s and the Deutscher Raiffeisenverband federates thousands of agricultural cooperatives.
ag.equipment_note: Eco-scheme and agri-environment payments (EUR 40 to 1,300/ha) are the most accessible money for a small diversified farm; investment grants for buildings and machinery exist under the Laender's agricultural investment programmes within the GAK framework but require a full-time farm business plan and co-financing, so a new commune should budget on CAP area payments only until it qualifies as an established farm.

legal.text: Genossenschaft (very strong co-op law), eingetragener Verein, Stiftung

vehicles.name: Eingetragene Genossenschaft (eG) under the Genossenschaftsgesetz (GenG, 1889)
vehicles.note: The standard German commune vehicle: at least 3 members (section 4 GenG), one member one vote, open membership, may pursue economic, social or cultural purposes (section 1 GenG), limited liability, can own farmland and buildings and run the farm; mandatory membership in a Pruefungsverband with periodic audits adds cost but also credibility with banks. Used by Sieben Linden (Siedlungsgenossenschaft Oekodorf eG), Schloss Tempelhof eG, Schloss Tonndorf eG and SelbstBau eG at Hof Praedikow; agricultural eGs are corporate-tax exempt under section 5(1) no. 14 KStG.

vehicles.name: Eingetragener Verein (e.V.) under sections 21 ff. BGB
vehicles.note: Non-commercial association gaining legal personality by entry in the Vereinsregister (section 21 BGB); cheap, 7 founders customary, can hold land and be recognised as gemeinnuetzig (charitable) for education, ecology or culture; not suited to running a commercial farm as its main purpose, so communities pair an e.V. (membership, seminars, donations) with an eG or GmbH (land and business), as at Sieben Linden, Tempelhof and Hof Praedikow.

vehicles.name: Rechtsfaehige Stiftung (foundation) under sections 80 ff. BGB, incl. the Stiftung trias model
vehicles.note: Member-less legal person endowed to pursue a founder-set purpose permanently (section 80 BGB; Verbrauchsstiftung variant may spend down capital); state recognition required. The purpose-bound asset lock makes it the German analogue of a community land trust: Stiftung trias buys land and grants a long Erbbaurecht to the resident cooperative (Hof Praedikow since 2017), and Tempelhof runs a Stiftung am Tempelhof alongside its eG and e.V.

vehicles.name: Erbbaurecht (heritable building right) under the ErbbauRG
vehicles.note: A transferable, inheritable right to have a building on another's land (section 1 ErbbauRG), registered in the land register for typically 66 to 99 years; lets a Stiftung or Landgesellschaft keep the land off the market while residents or their eG own and finance the buildings; the de facto German CLT mechanism and the one used at Hof Praedikow and (as Erbpacht plots) at Eden Oranienburg since 1893.

vehicles.name: GmbH / gGmbH, including the Mietshaeuser Syndikat house-project model
vehicles.note: Limited company (EUR 25,000 capital, or UG with less) that can own land and run any business; a gGmbH is charitable (ZEGG operates as ZEGG gGmbH). The Mietshaeuser Syndikat (Freiburg, 1992; 191 projects, about 3,800 residents by June 2024) uses a Haus-GmbH owned 51 percent by the residents' Hausverein and 49 percent by the Syndikat GmbH, with each side holding a veto on sale, which permanently removes the property from the market; several rural projects (Hof Praedikow-type estates) use it.

vehicles.name: Trust
vehicles.note: Germany has no common-law trust; foreign trusts holding German land face transparency and inheritance-tax problems. Use a Stiftung or the Syndikat GmbH veto structure instead.

zoning.text: Foreigners buy freely; strict building code; farmland transfer regulated
zoning.build_on_farmland: Restrictive. Land outside a Bebauungsplan or the built-up village area is Aussenbereich under section 35 BauGB, where new buildings are permitted only for 'privileged' uses: a dwelling or barn that 'serves an agricultural or forestry business and occupies a subordinate part of its land' (section 35(1) no. 1), horticulture, renewable energy and similar; a residential eco-village is not privileged, and non-privileged projects are approved only case by case if they impair no public interests (section 35(2)), which planning offices routinely deny. Conversions of preserved farm buildings are allowed (section 35(4)) up to 5 additional dwellings per farmstead if the exterior is kept and abandonment was under 7 years. Practical routes: buy an existing Hofstelle or village plots inside the Innenbereich, convert barns, or persuade the municipality to adopt a Bebauungsplan for the project (the path taken by Sieben Linden and Tempelhof). Each Land's Bauordnung also requires building permits for anything but the smallest sheds; tiny houses and yurts as permanent dwellings need permits like any house.
zoning.communal_title: Communal ownership is straightforward: an eG, e.V., GmbH or Stiftung can be the registered owner, and co-ownership by individuals (Bruchteile) is possible but makes GrdstVG approval and financing harder. Transfers of agricultural land above state thresholds (0.15 to 2 ha) need GrdstVG approval; approval can be refused for an 'unhealthy distribution' when a non-farmer buys land a local farmer wants, for splitting agricultural parcels below 1 ha, or for a price grossly above market; the Landgesellschaft has a pre-emption right on parcels of 2 ha or more when approval would be refused (section 4 RSiedlG). Baden-Wuerttemberg applies its own ASVG. A community that is itself a registered farm business avoids most of these objections.
zoning.note: Section 35 BauGB is the single biggest practical obstacle for new rural communes in Germany: ownership of farmland does not bring any right to live on it. Budget 12 to 36 months for a municipal Bebauungsplan if a greenfield settlement is the goal, and expect building-code, fire-safety and wastewater standards comparable to any German new build.

climate.zone: Temperate oceanic (Koeppen Cfb) in the west and north grading to humid continental (Dfb) in the east and the Alpine foreland; annual precipitation about 515 mm (Berlin/Brandenburg) to 945 mm (Munich), 800 mm on the North Sea coast; summer daily highs 22 to 25 C, winters mild in the west and cold in the east; growing season roughly April to October.
climate.risks: Main hazards are river and flash floods (July 2021 Ahr/Erft floods: at least 184 dead in Germany, EUR 33.4 billion direct damage, the deadliest natural disaster since 1962) and increasingly frequent summer droughts and heat (2018: grain harvest down about 20 percent, rapeseed down 30 percent, farmers requested over EUR 1 billion in aid; the sandy soils of Brandenburg and the eastern lowlands are most drought-prone). Wildfire risk is rising in Brandenburg pine forests; the last German glacier is disappearing. ND-GAIN ranks Germany 3rd globally (score 69.2; vulnerability 0.301, readiness 0.682), so adaptive capacity is among the best anywhere.
climate.water: Generally water-rich with abundant groundwater and a dense river network; irrigation is rare except in Brandenburg and parts of Lower Saxony, where abstraction permits are now contested after the 2018-2022 dry years. Choose river-terrace or loess soils in the west and south for reliable rainfall, or expect to invest in rainwater retention and drought-tolerant rotations on the cheap sandy eastern land.

commune_history: Germany's communal-settlement tradition is long and legally entrenched: the Raiffeisen rural cooperatives of the 1860s led to the Genossenschaftsgesetz of 1889, the vegetarian Lebensreform colony Eden at Oranienburg was founded in 1893 by 18 Berliners as a cooperative holding 125 ha with Erbpacht garden plots and still exists today as Eden Gemeinnuetzige Obstbau-Siedlung eG with about 1,500 residents, and the Reichssiedlungsgesetz of 1919 created the non-profit Landgesellschaften whose pre-emption rights still shape farmland sales. After 1968 the Kommune movement produced income-sharing communes such as Kommune Niederkaufungen (1986) and the Kommuja network, the Mietshaeuser Syndikat (Freiburg, 1992) built a replicable anti-speculation GmbH model now spanning 191 projects, and post-reunification cheap eastern land enabled ZEGG (1991), Sieben Linden (1997), Schloss Tonndorf (2005) and Hof Praedikow (2017, Stiftung trias plus Erbbaurecht plus cooperative). A new group can point to these as fully recognised precedents, including municipalities that adopted dedicated development plans for ecovillages, and to the 2006 GenG amendment that expressly allows social and cultural cooperatives.
dealbreakers: Section 35 BauGB: owning farmland gives no right to live on it; new homes outside a village or Bebauungsplan are only allowed for a bona fide farm business, so a greenfield ecovillage needs a municipal development plan (12 to 36 months, political) or an existing farmstead to convert.

No passive-income, retiree, golden or nomad visa for non-EU members; each adult needs an individual permit (section 21 business, Blue Card/skilled worker, or discretionary section 7) and private health insurance that insurers can refuse to older or sick applicants.

Farmland costs EUR 35,300/ha on average (EUR 15,000 in the east) and sales to non-farmers can be refused under the Grundstueckverkehrsgesetz or pre-empted by the Landgesellschaft when a local farmer wants the parcel.

Worldwide taxation at up to 47.5 percent with full taxation of foreign pensions from 2025 and a planned 25 percent flat crypto tax from 2027, plus mandatory cooperative audits and German-language bureaucracy at every step.
